lesson.title: Compound Builder Workshop
lesson.subtitle: Assemble compounds from taught nouns — and predict gender from the head

hook.title: You Are the Factory Now
hook.content: You have split compounds; today you build them. The parts are all on your bench: Zahn, Donner, Tag, Apfel, Buch, Haus, Kind, Garten. The rules are two: glue the nouns in meaning order (the modifier first, the head last), and let the head word donate the gender. Zahn + Arzt = der Zahnarzt. Donner + Tag = der Donnerstag. Apfel + Kuchen (a hint-word) = der Apfelkuchen. Build wrong and German speakers will still understand you — compounding is productive grammar, not fixed vocabulary — but the head-word law keeps your articles honest.

footnotes.title: German Lets You Coin
footnotes.content: Compound building is live grammar: a German can invent an absurdly long machine name and be understood. English does this too ('toothbrush holder') — German just never stopped showing the seams in writing.

pattern.title: Build, Then Predict
pattern.content: Build: Kind + Garten = der Kindergarten (the head Garten donates der — and English borrowed it whole). Donner + Tag = der Donnerstag. Zahn + Arzt = der Zahnarzt. Haus + Tür = die Haustür (die Tür is the head — the door, not the house). Wasser + Glas = das Wasserglas (a glass of water as an object). Reverse-engineer: die Eisenbahn splits Eisen (iron) + Bahn (track) — der/die/das is your split hint. Then the workshop trick: if you know the head, you know the article before you know the compound.
pattern.linguist_note: Sometimes a linking -s- or -e- sneaks in between the parts. The glue is historical spelling, not grammar — learn compounds whole once they are coined.

vocab_hints.note: birth-day takes der Tag's article — the day is the head

exercises.explanation: Geburt + Tag = der Geburtstag — the head word Tag donates the masculine article. Then feiern carries the party: Wir feiern den Geburtstag. Zahnarzt built the same way last lesson.

exercises.prompt: You coin 'Buchhaus' (a house of books). Which article?
options: das — Haus is the head word
exercises.target_answer: das — Haus is the head word
exercises.meaning: das Buchhaus — the head donates the gender
exercises.explanation: Modifier first, head last: Haus runs the grammar, so das Buchhaus. Hauptstadt works the same way (die Stadt is the head), and Heimweh weaves a feeling: Heim + Weh, home-woe.

exercises.prompt: Match the built compound with its English meaning:
exercises.target_answer: der Donnerstag, der Zahnarzt, der Apfelkuchen, der Kindergarten, der Fußball, der Regenbogen
exercises.meaning: Thursday, dentist, apple cake, kindergarten, football, rainbow
exercises.explanation: All six end in masculine heads — Tag, Arzt, Kuchen, Garten, Ball, Bogen — so all six wear der.

exercises.prompt: Split it: 'die Haustür' — what is the head word?
options: die Tür (the door) — so it is die Haustür
exercises.target_answer: die Tür (the door) — so it is die Haustür
exercises.explanation: The door is the thing being named; the house only says which one. Head word = die Tür → die Haustür.

vocab_hints.note: am = an + dem — the dative of time

exercises.explanation: Compound subject (der Geburtstag — Tag's article), dative of time (am Freitag), verb glued at 2.

summary.outcome: Coin compounds from taught nouns and predict their articles via the head word.
summary.takeaway: Modifier first, head last — and the head word donates gender, plural, and meaning core.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: reading compounds in the wild — six-word monsters, split into meaning.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Compound Builder Workshop (The birthday is on Friday):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Geburtstag ist am Freitag" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Compound Builder Workshop without relying on short-term echo.

donner.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Living in English "Thursday" (Thor's/Thunder's day = Donnerstag) and Santa's reindeer "Donner and Blitzen" (Thunder and Lightning).

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

geburtstag.etymology_derivation: Geburt + Tag, exactly English birthday; the Tag/day pair shows the d to t stop shift, and Geburt comes from the gebären family. [wiktionary]

feiern.context_translation: We are celebrating a birthday today.
feiern.etymology_derivation: From Old High German firOn, from fira, from Latin feriae (festival days) - the same Latin word that became the English fair, a market held on feast days. [wiktionary][etymonline]

zahnarzt.context_translation: The dentist looks at my teeth.
zahnarzt.etymology_derivation: Zahn (tooth) + Arzt (doctor) - literally tooth-doctor; Zahn shows the t-to-z shift from the same ancient root as English tooth (PIE *h₃dónts). [wiktionary]

hauptstadt.context_phrase: Berlin ist die Hauptstadt von Deutschland.
hauptstadt.context_translation: Berlin is the capital of Germany.
hauptstadt.etymology_derivation: Haupt + Stadt, literally head city; the page traces Haupt to the PIE head root that also yields Latin caput, so English capital is the Latin twin, and Stadt is the twin of English stead. [wiktionary]

fußball.etymology_derivation: Fuß + Ball — a calque of English football; Fuß is foot with the t→s shift. [wiktionary]

regenbogen.context_phrase: Nach dem Regen sehen wir einen Regenbogen.
regenbogen.context_translation: After the rain we see a rainbow.
regenbogen.etymology_derivation: Regen (rain) plus Bogen (bow — twin of English bow); the page lists English rainbow as the parallel cognate — the exact same compound. [wiktionary]

heimweh.context_phrase: Nach einer Woche hatte sie Heimweh.
heimweh.context_translation: After a week she was homesick.
heimweh.etymology_derivation: Heim (home, Proto-Germanic *haimaz) + Weh (pain, from the root behind English woe): home-woe, homesickness. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
